result.markdown: --- title: "Standard Normal (μ = 0, σ = 1)" subtitle: "The control case: a population that is already normal" --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Show the simulation code"} source("../R/clt_functions.R") rgen <- function(n) rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1) mu <- 0 sigma <- 1 coarse <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100) exper <- run_with_refinement(rgen, coarse, mu, sigma) res <- exper$results n_main <- smallest_normal_n(res) n_std <- n_by_standard(res) at <- function(k) res[res$n == k, ] save_results(res, "normal") save_summary(res, "Normal(0,1)", n_main, prediction = "1", key_note = "Control case: normal at every n") ``` ::: ::: {.answer-box} n = 1 under my main standard (strict standard: 1 · lenient standard: 1 · my prediction: 1) ::: ## 1. What population am I sampling from? The standard normal distribution: the bell curve itself. It is symmetric, has no skewness, and its tails are exactly as heavy as the normal benchmark. It is the **control case** of the study: if the simulation and the diagnostics work correctly, the sample means should pass every check at every sample size. | Property | Value | |---|---| | Mean μ | 0 | | Standard deviation σ | 1 | | Skewness | 0 | | Excess kurtosis | 0 | | Theoretical SE of the mean | 1/√n | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(student_id) style_par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1)) x <- rnorm(100000) hist(x, breaks = 60, freq = FALSE, col = adjustcolor(pal$bars, 0.75), border = "white", main = "", xlab = "Value", ylab = "Density") curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, col = pal$curve, lwd = 2.2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The population: 100,000 draws from N(0, 1) with the true density.](01_normal_files/figure-html/fig-population-1.png){#fig-population width=990} ::: ::: ## 2. What did I expect before running the simulation? > **n = 1.** The population is already normal, and in my pilot run every check passed at n = 1. > A mean of independent normal values is itself exactly normal, so there is nothing to wait for. ## 3. Which sample sizes did I investigate? n = 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, with **B = 100,000** sample means per n and seed 9426. Since n = 1 already passes, no refinement stage was needed. ## 4. Results ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_convergence(res, chosen_n = n_main, theory_skew = 0, theory_kurt = 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The four checks stay inside the pass zone at every n.](01_normal_files/figure-html/fig-convergence-1.png){#fig-convergence width=990} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_hist_grid(exper, c(1, 5, 30), mu, sigma) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sampling distribution of the mean (bars) and the CLT normal curve (red).](01_normal_files/figure-html/fig-hist-1.png){#fig-hist width=990} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_qq_grid(exper, c(1, 5, 30)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Normal Q-Q plots: straight lines at every n.](01_normal_files/figure-html/fig-qq-1.png){#fig-qq width=990} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_se_check(res) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Simulated SE (dots) against σ/√n (line).](01_normal_files/figure-html/fig-se-1.png){#fig-se width=990} ::: ::: The simulated mean stayed within 0.0021 of 0, and the simulated SE stayed within 0.6% of 1/√n at every sample size. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## 5. When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal? $$\boxed{n = 1}$$ ::: {#tbl-standards .cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Standard | Max |skewness|| Smallest n| |:----------------------|------------------------:|----------:| |Strict | 0.10| 1| |**Main (my standard)** | 0.25| **1**| |Lenient | 0.50| 1| ::: ::: ## 6. Why did I choose that value? - At n = 1 the skewness is -0.008, the excess kurtosis -0.014, the Q-Q correlation 1.0000, and the tails are 2.55% / 2.48%, all essentially perfect. The same holds at every larger n. - Even the Shapiro-Wilk test, which I do not use for decisions because it is very sensitive, rejected normality at the 5% level for only 0 of the 9 sample sizes. That is about what chance alone would produce for truly normal data. - This confirms the tools: on data that really are normal, my simulation and my four checks do not create false alarms. That makes the failures in the other populations meaningful. ## 7. What surprised me? > This one was not a surprise. The sample means were normal already at n = 1 under all three standards, > which makes sense because averaging normal values always gives a normal result. It was also a useful > check that my simulation code was not distorting anything.
